channel.title: California Uzbek — Latest
channel.description: Independent analysis · Central Asia & world geopolitics

item.title: Iran says it struck a US radar in Bahrain; the US denies it
item.description: The IRGC announced it had destroyed a US early-warning radar in Bahrain; US Central Command said two drones were shot down and nothing was damaged. Iran called it a response to a strike on Sirik.

item.title: Uzbekistan identifies 12 human rights challenges linked to business activities
item.description: At its first National Dialogue on Business and Human Rights, an assessment presented by the National Human Rights Centre and UNDP identified 12 key challenges including labour rights, workplace safety, informal employment and environmental protection.

item.title: Uzbekistan's Mirziyoyev ranks 40th on the world's 500 most influential Muslims
item.description: In the 2027 edition of The Muslim 500, Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev is ranked 40th — the highest among Central Asian leaders; he is 18th in the politicians category.

item.title: Britain overhauls settlement: the standard route rises from 5 to 10 years
item.description: Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood announced an 'earned settlement' reform — permanent residence will depend on salary, English and contribution; around 500,000 people will qualify later than under current rules.

item.title: A UK anti-migrant activist admits slashing a migrant boat in the English Channel
item.description: Daniel Thomas, 37, pleaded guilty to criminal damage at Portsmouth Crown Court. In the 22 September incident the roughly 50 migrants had already been rescued; only a French coast-guard officer remained aboard. Sentencing is on Wednesday.

item.title: In Australia, political parties are presenting themselves as 'independent news' accounts
item.description: An Instagram account, @nswnewsroom, looks like a media outlet's newsfeed, but it was set up by the NSW Labor party. An expert called it a legal 'loophole'. Similar pages exist for the Liberals and the Climate 200 group.

item.title: The British Council marks 30 years in Uzbekistan: 1.7 million participants and about ten UK universities
item.description: The British Council has operated in Uzbekistan since 1996. Over 30 years its programmes have reached 1.7 million direct participants, and its initiatives have reached 42 million people. Today more than 10,000 students earn a British diploma inside Uzbekistan.

item.title: Report: China's diaspora-control network reaches deep into Europe
item.description: Madrid-based Safeguard Defenders says the Chinese Communist Party monitors its diaspora through 1,247 'liaison points' in at least 91 countries, hundreds of them in Europe; the network has 'persuaded' about 230,000 people to return to China.

item.title: The Irani of Uzbekistan: history of the Persian-speaking Shia community deported from Merv
item.description: The 'Irani' (or 'Ironi') are a Persian-speaking Shia community living around Samarkand and Bukhara. Most trace their origin to the city of Merv (Mary) in today's Turkmenistan. In 1785 the Bukharan emir Shah Murad captured Merv, destroyed its irrigation dam, and resettled the city's population — about 100,000 people — in stages to the oases of Bukhara and Samarkand. Persian-speaking and Shia, this community preserved its language and school of law among a Sunni majority. A historical reference — facts only.

item.title: How Ponzi and pyramid schemes work — and how to spot them
item.description: Ponzi and pyramid schemes are financial fraud disguised as investment. In both, the 'returns' come not from real profit but from the money of newly recruited people; when fresh money stops coming in, the scheme collapses. In a Ponzi scheme investors are passive — a central operator promises fake returns; in a pyramid scheme the participant earns by recruiting new members. The name comes from Charles Ponzi, who promised 50% returns in the United States in 1920; the largest Ponzi in history was the Bernard Madoff case (~$65 billion). A reference — facts only.

item.title: Islamic rulings explained: fard, wajib, sunnah, mustahabb, mubah, makruh and haram
item.description: In Islamic jurisprudence every act is placed into five — or, in the Hanafi school, seven — categories: fard, wajib, sunnah, mustahabb, mubah, makruh and haram. These define how obligatory or forbidden an act is, and the reward or sin in doing or leaving it. The Hanafi school (followed by most in Uzbekistan and the diaspora) distinguishes fard from wajib, while the other schools often treat them as the same. A reference — facts only, not a fatwa.

item.title: Uzbekistan joins the Organisation of the Islamic Conference (1995–1996)
item.description: After independence, Uzbekistan restored formal ties with the Muslim world. At an extraordinary meeting of foreign ministers held in New York in the autumn of 1995, Uzbekistan was admitted to the Organisation of the Islamic Conference (OIC) as an observer, and on 2 October 1996 it became a full member. This was part of the country's religious revival and its multi-vector foreign policy. In 2011 the organisation was renamed the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation. A historical reference — facts only.

item.title: A London court finds two Iranian men guilty of surveilling journalists
item.description: Woolwich Crown Court found Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, and Farhad Javadi Manesh, 46, guilty of assisting Iran's intelligence service; they had surveilled journalists of Iran International in London. Sentencing is on 17 December.

item.title: Kenyan domestic worker sentenced to 100 lashes in Saudi Arabia
item.description: According to court documents reviewed by The New York Times, a 40-year-old Kenyan woman was sentenced in Riyadh to 100 lashes and one year of banishment for giving birth outside marriage; Saudi authorities did not confirm the sentence.

item.title: Uyghurs in Uzbekistan: migration from East Turkestan and the formation of the community
item.description: The Uyghurs are a Turkic people close to Uzbeks in language and culture, historically tied to East Turkestan (present-day northwestern China — Xinjiang). The Uyghur community in Uzbekistan took shape through centuries of Silk Road trade, migration from Kashgar and movements in the Soviet period. A notable fact: the ethnonym 'Uyghur' was adopted in its modern sense in Tashkent in 1921. History, facts only; population figures are estimates.

item.title: Uzbekistan-Iran diplomatic relations (1991-1996): the establishment of early ties
item.description: Iran was among the first states to recognize independent Uzbekistan: recognition came in December 1991, and diplomatic relations were formally established on 10 May 1992 (by a protocol signed in Ashgabat). The early years revolved around trade, transit and a shared Persianate cultural heritage, while Tashkent pursued a cautious policy as a secular state. History, facts only; some exact dates are approximate.

item.title: Germany's Deutsche Bahn offers Uzbek construction workers jobs starting at €3,418 a month
item.description: Germany's national rail operator is recruiting construction specialists through Uzbekistan's Migration Agency: a starting gross salary of €3,418, 30 days of paid leave and free German-language training in Tashkent.

item.title: How US Medicare and Medicaid work: the two public health-coverage systems
item.description: Medicare is a FEDERAL insurance mainly for people 65+ and certain people with disabilities (based on age/disability); Medicaid is a joint FEDERAL-STATE program for low-income people (income-based, with rules that vary by state). This reference explains, facts only, how they differ, their parts, their costs (with 2026 figures) and — crucially — the rules for immigrants, including the 5-year bar and the public-charge rule that changed in September 2026.

item.title: How the Qurʼan is structured and was revealed: suras, verses, juzʼ and the basics of recitation
item.description: The Qurʼan has 114 suras and, in the Hafs reading, about 6,236 verses, divided into 30 juzʼ for reading. It was revealed to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) over roughly 23 years (610–632) through the angel Gabriel. This reference explains, within mainstream, widely accepted scholarship and facts only, the Qurʼan's structure, revelation, compilation and the basics of its recitation.

item.title: South Korea expands farm technology in Uzbekistan: rice, dairy and strawberries
item.description: South Korea's Rural Development Administration (RDA) has cut manual labour in rice planting by about 70% in Uzbekistan; cooperation is also growing in dairy breeding and greenhouse strawberries.

item.title: One in three Germans backs anti-Muslim statements, Leipzig study finds
item.description: The University of Leipzig's 2026 Authoritarianism Study: anti-Muslim attitudes reach 34.1%, right-wing extremism has doubled, and satisfaction with democracy is at the lowest level in the survey's history.

item.title: Israel detains foreign activists who helped Palestinian farmers in the occupied West Bank
item.description: Israeli forces detained international volunteers aiding the olive harvest in the occupied West Bank and ordered a group deported; the Israeli group Yesh Din recorded 672 settler attacks in five weeks.

item.title: Forced labour persists in Turkmenistan's cotton harvest
item.description: Teachers, doctors and state employees are forced to pick cotton or to pay from their salaries for a replacement; reform pledges are not being met.

item.title: Uzbekistan joins the Economic Cooperation Organization (ECO), 1992
item.description: On 28 November 1992 Uzbekistan, together with six other newly independent states, joined the Economic Cooperation Organization (ECO) founded by Iran, Pakistan and Turkey. The step opened sea-access routes and regional trade corridors for the young state — the organization's history, aims and significance for Uzbekistan, facts only.

item.title: Halal investing: how stocks are screened for Shari'ah compliance
item.description: Why buying a share differs from a bond, how shares are vetted through a two-step Shari'ah screen (business activity and financial ratios), how the AAOIFI, Dow Jones Islamic Market and MSCI standards differ, and what dividend "purification" (tat-hir) means — a facts-only explainer.

item.title: Trump: Israel and Gulf allies should repay the cost of the Iran war
item.description: In a CBS '60 Minutes' interview the US president said the countries it protects should repay the cost of the 2026 Iran war; analysts called it political rhetoric.

item.title: The second hijra of Uzbek émigrés from Afghanistan (1979–1992): a "doubly displaced" community
item.description: The descendants of Turkestani émigrés who fled Soviet rule into northern Afghanistan in the 1920s–30s were forced to flee again from the 1979 Soviet invasion — to Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey. The history of an Uzbek community that became refugees twice within a few generations, facts only.

item.title: Uzbekistan's annual inflation reached 6.5% in October
item.description: According to the Statistics Committee, prices rose 0.6% over the month; fuel, propane, meat and transport rose sharply.

item.title: Russia, Ukraine and the US begin talks in Abu Dhabi
item.description: The first trilateral meeting since February; the two-day session focused on future security guarantees.

item.title: How news media make money, and how bias arises
item.description: "Follow the money": advertising, subscriptions, membership, state funding and syndication — the revenue sources of media outlets and how each creates a slant (bias) in story selection, explained facts-only. A media-literacy explainer.
